title: The Song of Moses: The Rock and His Wayward People
summary: Moses sings a long poem calling heaven and earth to hear. It praises the LORD as the faithful Rock, recalls how he found Israel in the wilderness and cared for them like an eagle with its young, and then describes how Israel grew fat and turned to other gods, provoking God's anger and judgment. Yet the song ends with God vindicating his people and taking vengeance on his enemies. Afterward Moses urges Israel to take these words to heart, and God tells him to climb Mount Nebo, view the land, and die.
story: Chapter 31 told Moses to write a song that would testify against Israel when they turned away. This is that song. It functions as a prophetic summary of Israel's whole history before it happens: God's kindness, Israel's ingratitude, judgment, and finally God's compassion and rescue. It gives later generations words to understand their own disasters. The closing prose (verses 44-52) returns to the plains of Moab and sets up the last scenes of Deuteronomy: Moses' blessing of the tribes in chapter 33 and his death on Mount Nebo in chapter 34.
historical:
The song is presented as Moses' own composition at the end of the wilderness period, whose date follows the debated date of the exodus. Scholars have long discussed the poem's age on other grounds. Its archaic Hebrew features have led many to regard it as one of the older poems in the Old Testament, though estimates range widely, from early in Israel's history to the period of the monarchy or later. Critical scholars often see it as reflecting a time of foreign oppression, while those who hold to Mosaic authorship read it as prophecy. Either way, its pattern fits what followed: Israel settled in a fertile land, adopted the worship of Canaanite gods such as Baal, and suffered invasion and exile at the hands of Assyria and Babylon.

The closing verses recall a specific event. At the waters of Meribah-kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin (Numbers 20:1-13), Moses struck the rock instead of speaking to it, and God said that he and Aaron had not treated him as holy before the people. Aaron died on Mount Hor (Numbers 20:22-29). Moses now learns that he too will die outside the land, on Mount Nebo in the Abarim range of Moab, from which he can see across the Jordan toward Jericho.
cultural:
Songs were how ancient peoples remembered. Israel had already sung at the Red Sea (Exodus 15), and later the prophets would use poetry to bring God's case against his people. This song has the shape of what scholars call a covenant lawsuit: heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses (verse 1), the plaintiff's faithfulness is declared (verse 4), the accused's ingratitude is described (verses 5-18), and a verdict follows (verses 19-42). Prophets like Isaiah (chapter 1) and Micah (chapter 6) used the same form.

The picture of God as the Rock (tsur) runs through the poem. In a land of cliffs and wilderness, a rock meant shelter, defense, and stability. The song contrasts Israel's Rock with the rocks of the nations, the gods in which they took refuge (verses 31, 37). Verse 8 reflects an ancient belief found across the Near East that the nations were divided among heavenly beings. The Hebrew text preserved in medieval manuscripts (the Masoretic Text) reads that God set boundaries according to the number of the sons of Israel, while a Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy and the Greek Septuagint support a reading with sons of God or angels of God, which the BSB follows. On that reading, other nations were assigned to lesser heavenly powers, but the LORD kept Israel as his own portion (verse 9).
literary: The song is Hebrew poetry built on parallel lines, where the second line echoes, extends, or sharpens the first: “Let my teaching fall like rain and my speech settle like dew” (verse 2). It moves in clear stages: summons (verses 1-3), God's faithfulness and Israel's corruption (verses 4-6), God's past care (verses 7-14), Israel's rebellion (verses 15-18), God's decision to judge (verses 19-27), a lament over Israel's folly (verses 28-33), and God's vindication of his people (verses 34-43). The word Rock recurs as a structural thread. Striking images of care (the eagle stirring its nest, honey from the rock) give way to images of judgment (fire burning to the depths of Sheol, arrows, famine, wild beasts). Verses 26 and 27 are a turning point: God holds back from total destruction because the enemy would boast that its own hand had won. The song ends not with Israel's ruin but with a call for the nations to rejoice with God's people.

outline.t: Heaven and earth summoned to hear
The faithful Rock and a crooked generation
God's care for Israel from the wilderness to the land
Jeshurun grows fat and forgets the Rock
God resolves to judge, but holds back
Israel's folly and the enemies' poison
Vengeance belongs to God: his people vindicated
Take these words to heart: they are your life
Moses told to climb Nebo and die

doctrines.note: God is the Rock whose work is perfect, just, faithful, and upright (verse 4). His character is the fixed point against which Israel's unfaithfulness is measured.

Prosperity leads Israel to forget God and turn to new gods and demons (verses 15-18). The song treats idolatry as ingratitude and betrayal, provoking God's jealousy, which in Scripture is the rightful zeal of a husband or father for a relationship that belongs to him.
God's judgment is real and severe, but it serves his purposes: he refuses to let enemies claim victory, and he takes vengeance on those who hate him. Vengeance belongs to God, not to people.
Verse 39 is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements that there is no God besides the LORD, who brings death and gives life, wounds and heals.

words.note: Tsur, rock. The song calls God the Rock again and again (verses 4, 15, 18, 30, 31) and mocks the rock in which the nations took refuge (verse 37). The image stands for strength, refuge, and permanence. Later psalms often call God my rock, drawing on this language.

Jeshurun, a poetic name for Israel, probably from the root meaning upright. Its use in verse 15 is ironic: the upright one grew fat and kicked. It appears again in Deuteronomy 33 and once in Isaiah 44:2.

Qana, to be jealous or zealous. Israel provokes God's jealousy with foreign gods, and God answers by making Israel jealous through a people who are not a people (verse 21). Paul quotes this in Romans 10:19 when he explains the inclusion of the Gentiles.

Naqam, vengeance. In the Bible vengeance is not private revenge but the rightful act of a judge restoring justice. The song reserves it for God, which is why Paul quotes verse 35 in Romans 12:19 to tell believers not to avenge themselves.

christ: The New Testament uses this song often. Paul quotes verse 21 in Romans 10:19 to show that God had long ago said he would stir Israel's jealousy through those who were not a nation, and he quotes verse 43 in Romans 15:10, “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people,” as part of his case that the gospel was always meant to gather the nations. Hebrews 1:6 applies the line “Let all God’s angels worship Him” from verse 43 (in its longer Greek and Dead Sea Scroll form) to Christ, the firstborn. Romans 12:19 and Hebrews 10:30 cite verse 35 on God's vengeance. Paul's warning in 1 Corinthians 10:20 that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons echoes verse 17, and Philippians 2:15 echoes the crooked and perverse generation of verse 5. Most striking is verse 39, where God alone kills and makes alive; the New Testament proclaims that this God raised Jesus from the dead. The song also points ahead to Moses' own limits: he cannot enter the land, a reminder that the one who gave the law could not bring the people into final rest.

hard.q: How should we read a song about God's arrows drunk with blood and his vengeance on enemies?
hard.a: The imagery of verses 23-25 and 41-42 is violent, and it can be troubling. A few points help. First, this is poetry using the conventional images of ancient warfare to express the seriousness of God's justice, and much of the violence described (famine, plague, the sword) falls on Israel itself as covenant judgment, not on outsiders alone. Second, the song insists that vengeance belongs to God precisely so that it does not belong to people; the New Testament draws that conclusion directly (Romans 12:19). Third, the song ends in compassion: God vindicates his servants when their strength is gone, and the nations are called to rejoice. Some readers stress God's holy anger against evil as something to be taken seriously rather than softened; others emphasize that such language belongs to a lament-and-hope genre that expresses trust that God will set things right. Both agree the song is not a license for human violence.

questions: The song says Israel grew fat and forgot the God who made them. How can comfort and success make it easier to forget God?
God is called the Rock again and again. What do you tend to lean on for stability in place of God?
Moses says these words are not idle words but your life (verse 47). What would it look like to treat God's word that seriously?
